subtitle: How to operate DNS when queries travel over both IPv4 and IPv6 networks.

tldr.problem: When DNS is deployed across mixed IPv4 and IPv6 networks, there is a risk that some DNS zones become reachable only over IPv6, fragmenting the DNS name space and breaking lookups for IPv4-only clients.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3901 recommends administrative policies: every recursive name server should be either IPv4-only or dual-stack (never IPv6-only), and every DNS zone should be served by at least one IPv4-reachable authoritative name server.
tldr.outcome: The guidelines prevent name space fragmentation during the IPv4-to-IPv6 transition, ensuring that all clients can reach all zones regardless of their IP version.

today: RFC 3901 is a Best Current Practice guideline that was made Historic and replaced by RFC 10001. Its core principle—that DNS zones must remain accessible over IPv4—remains important for DNS interoperability.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3901 addresses the challenges of operating DNS during the transition from IPv4 to a mixed IPv4 and IPv6 Internet. DNS resolution normally starts at the root and follows referrals down a chain of name servers until reaching one authoritative for the requested name. If any server in the chain is reachable only over a transport (IPv4 or IPv6) that the resolver cannot use, the lookup fails.

As the Internet transitions to support both IPv4 and IPv6, there is a risk of DNS name space fragmentation, where some zones become accessible only over IPv6 while others remain only on IPv4. RFC 3901 provides Best Current Practice guidelines to prevent this.
sections.eli5: When looking up a name, your computer follows directions through many servers. If any server only listens on a language your computer doesn't speak, you get lost. This explains how to stop that.

sections.title: The Name Space Fragmentation Problem
sections.content:
During steady-state IPv4-only deployment, all DNS data is available over IPv4, making lookups straightforward. During IPv6-only deployment (if it occurred), all DNS data would be over IPv6. However, the real scenario is a transition where DNS data exists in three categories: available only over IPv4, only over IPv6, or on both transports.

The critical concern is preserving the IPv4 name space. It is not acceptable to break lookups for IPv4-only hosts by creating zones accessible only over IPv6. The challenge is to allow zones to move to IPv6 while maintaining backward compatibility and ensuring that all users—regardless of their transport capability—can continue to access the entire DNS name space.
sections.eli5: Imagine some shops only open for old-style phone calls, some only for new-style calls, and some for both. The rule is: make sure the old-style phones can still reach every shop, even if many shops add new-style phones.

sections.title: Recommended Guidelines
sections.content:
RFC 3901 recommends two key administrative policies. Every recursive name server should be either IPv4-only or dual-stack, never IPv6-only. This means that any resolver (including IPv6-only resolvers that cannot directly access all zones) can use a dual-stack recursive server as a forwarder. Every DNS zone should be served by at least one IPv4-reachable authoritative name server. This ensures that even if a zone has IPv6 name servers, IPv4-only clients can still resolve names in that zone.

Additionally, zone validation processes should ensure that child delegations point to at least one IPv4-reachable name server. These policies preserve the continuity of the DNS name space for all clients during the IPv4-to-IPv6 transition.
sections.eli5: Rule 1: All help desks (recursive servers) must handle both old and new calls, or just old calls. Rule 2: Every shop (zone) must have at least one old-style phone, so even old-phone-only customers can reach them.
